newsitem.title: USA: Multinationals walk legal tightrope abroad.
newsitem.headline: Multinationals walk legal tightrope abroad.

text.p: Human resources officials of U.S. companies abroad are being told to ignore foreign workplace hiring customs that are illegal in the United States.

Even when they must yield to foreign laws that conflict with U.S. statutes, they are expected to make a fight of it -- or run the risk of losing a damage lawsuit brought by an aggrieved job applicant or employee.

On paper, employees of U.S. businesses and their overseas affiliates who are U.S. citizens are shielded by civil rights laws relating to their age, race, religion, sex, national origin or disability. In reality, though, personnel managers who back an employee can land in hot water.

"If they don't (comply with U.S. law), they run the risk of liability," said attorney Michael Starr of Parker Chapin Flattau & Klimpl in New York, "and if they do, they may wind up doing things which are contrary" to foreign statutes.
"The global implications of these laws are not always clear or even uniform thoughout the United States" and are "still in the process of developing," Starr added.
"Businesses that fail to anticipate these developments may find themselves dragged into U.S. courts with little or no place to hide," he warned.
Starr estimated that approximately 21,000 units of 2,000 American transnational companies doing business abroad are affected.
To the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, "there is a fundamental difference between the customs and practices of a host country and its statutory mandates," Starr said.

In an article in The Business Lawyer, an American Bar Association journal, Starr wrote that the EEOC allows transnationals to invoke the so-called foreign law defence "only where compliance with U.S. discrimination laws will lead 'inevitably' to a violation of foreign law."

For example, Saudi Arabian law mandates beheading of any non-Moslem who flies over the holy city of Mecca -- adequate justification, Starr wrote, for a U.S. company to refuse to hire a non-Moslem helicopter pilot.

Again, when a German law provided for mandatory retirement of workers at age 65, the dismissal of two senior American employees by Radio Free Europe in Munich was upheld although it violated the U.S. Federal Age Discrimination in Employment Act.
Starr goes on to say that even when U.S. companies yield legally, "they may be required to show that they took all possible steps to obtain an exemption from host-country authorities."

And where custom, not law, is concerned, U.S. managers must run the risk of making decisions that are unpopular in their host country. For instance, a medical school was told by a U.S. court that it could not refuse to send a Jewish doctor to work in a Saudi Arabian hospital based on its "gleaned impressions" that Saudis do not want Jews there.
"I hope they (foreign governments) see that U.S. employment laws are grounded in something valuable for people," said Jim Klein of the Towers Perrin human resources consulting firm in New York.
When it comes to "the role of women, minorities, (and) age discrimination, we're (U.S.) way ahead of everybody else," Klein said.
Jack Raisner, a professor of business law at St. John's University in New York, believes that U.S. anti-bias law is having an educational impact globally.
"Over in Japan, they are scrambling to adapt to the experience they've had here on sexual harassment. There's an awareness that's spilling over into other countries," Raisner said.

According to Starr, "In the days of Yankee imperialism, it was sometimes said by xenophobic Americans that the U.S. Constitution followed the flag. Those days are gone, but the impulse to expand the reach of American standards of conduct persists." Not always, though, without a struggle.
(EDITORS: Sherwood Ross is a freelance writer who covers workplace issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Ross.)
